sections.heading: Devnet 8 Status and Attack Resilience
sections.summary: Devnet 8 ran stably over the weekend despite three attack variations; network kept finalizing and most clients process blocks within ~6 seconds.
sections.body:
- Devnet 8 has been running decently stable over the weekend, including through three different attack variations; Paweł was pointed to for the detail.
- The network stayed finalizing throughout; attacks did not significantly impact nodes, and ongoing client optimizations have continually improved robustness.
- Most clients can process blocks within approximately 6 seconds even in edge-case scenarios; some clients take slightly longer in certain scenarios.
- The security team found a bug in ethrex that caused memory explosion; it has already been fixed and all ethrex nodes are running smoothly again on devnet 8.
- Releases are being rolled out on devnet 8 to verify everything still works; after successful Sepolia fork, devnet 8 images will revert to latest trunk branches.

sections.heading: 200 Million Gas Limit Safety
sections.summary: Benchmarking confirms 200M gas is safe; slow devnet blocks were caused by debug tracing compounding with memory-intensive attacks, not by execution alone.
sections.body:
- Maria clarified confusion from the last ACDE where Potuz mixed up two different attacks that occurred at different times on devnet 8.
- Paweł's attacks were not producing slow blocks; worst case was 2.5 seconds execution time, confirmed both from devnet payloads and Benchmark Core results.
- Jochem's attack (also a JUMPDEST analysis vector) did cause slower blocks, but the root cause was out-of-memory issues from running memory-intensive attacks simultaneously with debug tracing enabled.
  - This combination is not expected on a normal validator.
- Benchmark Core (without debug tracing) does not show slow blocks for these attacks.
- Conclusion: 200 million gas is safe from an execution time perspective based on both benchmarks and devnet observations.
- The devnet has not yet been tested without debug tracing; agreement to run tests on devnet 8 with tracing disabled and also on a mainnet shadow fork.
  - Łukasz and others agreed this should be done to re-validate assumptions.
- Key difference between Benchmark Core and devnet: Benchmark Core only runs EL (no CL overhead), though it limits cores to account for CL resource usage.
- Csaba noted that network propagation effects are not captured in benchmarks and will only show on the network.

sections.heading: New Block Tag for Fast Confirmation Rule
sections.summary: Proposal to add a new block tag (likely "confirmed") instead of repurposing "safe" for FCR; can be implemented optionally without a hard fork.
sections.body:
- Julian Ma proposed creating a new block tag for fast-confirmed blocks instead of repurposing the existing `safe` tag, due to backwards compatibility issues hindering RPC provider adoption.
  - RPC providers want to continue serving justified blocks behind `safe` for existing customers, while also offering FCR — they need to serve both.
  - Chainlink announced going live with FCR; other bridges and L2s also want to use it.
  - Draft implementation by Mikhail already exists: [execution-apis PR #908](https://github.com/ethereum/execution-apis/pull/908).
- Dustin argued that justification/`safe` never had a stable definition — it changed partway through CL spec history — so repurposing it wouldn't break long-standing compatibility.
- Julian acknowledged Dustin's point but noted that empirically, large financial institutions rely on the `safe` tag with larger governance processes, making a new tag the pragmatic path.
- Tag naming discussion: `fast`, `fcr`, and `confirmed` were proposed.
  - Mikhail noted `fcr` is attached to a specific algorithm and slightly preferred against it, since in-protocol fast confirmation is coming with DC upgrade.
  - `confirmed` was suggested by Jihoon and drew strong support in chat from Justin Florentine, Enrico, cayman, Nico Flaig, and Justin Traglia.
- Mikhail asked whether this should be coordinated via a hard fork; consensus from Potuz and Enrico was that it does not require a hard fork.
  - It can be implemented as an optional feature: node operators who want FCR run compatible CL/EL pairs that support the new field.
  - The new field would simply not be present in FCU by default; CL only sends it when fast confirmation is enabled.
  - No change needed to the default node behavior for the vast majority of operators.
- Kev asked whether `safe` would eventually be deprecated; Julian said they would monitor adoption and let users decide — if people move away from `safe`, it could be deprecated eventually.
- Follow-up discussion to continue on the draft PR and ETH R&D Discord.

sections.heading: Genesis JSON Alloc Key Bug
sections.summary: Nethermind fails on genesis JSON without 0x prefix on alloc keys; PR in eth-clients repo needs client team approvals.
sections.body:
- Barnabas reported that the Glamsterdam genesis JSON file has alloc keys without the `0x` prefix.
- This bug was discovered during a mini shadow fork when Nethermind failed to parse the JSON file without the prefix.
  - The issue surfaced because they stopped using chainspec JSONs.
- A PR has been opened in the eth-clients repo: [mainnet PR #18](https://github.com/eth-clients/mainnet/pull/18).
- Each client team needs to review and approve before it can be merged.

sections.heading: Mainnet Bootnode Migration
sections.summary: EF is migrating mainnet bootnodes from PandaOps infrastructure to another EF team; PRs merged in most clients except Geth.
sections.body:
- Bootnodes previously managed by the PandaOps team are being handed over to another team within the EF, requiring infrastructure migration from one set of machines to another.
- PRs have been made and merged in most clients; Geth was flagged today as the remaining one.
  - Related PR: [mainnet PR #16](https://github.com/eth-clients/mainnet/pull/16).
- Existing old bootnodes will remain operational at least until mainnet Glamsterdam, when all clients have updated; old machines will then be deprecated.

sections.heading: JUMPDEST Analysis Attack: Devnet vs Benchmark Discrepancy
sections.summary: Devnet shows ~5s blocks for Paweł's JUMPDEST attack while Benchmark Core shows 2.5s; debug tracing, disk latency, and code cache eviction are suspected factors.
sections.body:
- Paweł flagged a block on devnet 8 using JUMPDEST analysis with 64KB contracts causing ~5 second execution at p90, especially when code caches are empty.
  - The block used approximately 100 million gas; doubling to 200 million could strain cores further.
- Benchmark Core shows worst-case 2.5 seconds for similar attacks — a significant discrepancy from devnet results.
- Multiple factors identified for the discrepancy:
  - Debug tracing enabled on devnet generates gigabytes of JSON output, adding overhead.
  - Devnet runs on cloud droplets with network-attached disks (not local NVMe), increasing I/O latency compared to Benchmark Core's dedicated hardware.
  - Paweł's attack loads ~4.4GB of contracts from disk, evicting code caches entirely (confirmed for Besu).
  - Benchmark Core's JUMPDEST test loads contracts directly into memory, skipping the disk-read bottleneck.
- Dragan (Reth) reported consistent ~5 second execution times on the flagged block; Reth plans optimizations that should significantly reduce this within days to a week.
- Maria argued against repricing JUMPDEST until tests are run without debug tracing, since Benchmark Core results don't warrant it.
- Ben Adams (Nethermind) noted pre-optimization benchmarks showed ~2 seconds on one core, now down to ~0.3 seconds — suggesting the analysis itself (not just disk loading) matters.
- Agreement to turn off debug tracing on devnet 8 and have Paweł re-run the attack.
  - Stefan will coordinate turning off tracing and reaching out to Paweł.
- Besu and Nethermind noted that their Sepolia release versions do not include latest trunk optimizations.
  - Besu's main branch has optimizations not in the Sepolia release; same for Nethermind.
  - PandaOps offered to swap back to trunk branches before running the test, which both teams preferred.
- Maria also asked about running Jochem's attack separately to validate.
- Follow-up discussion to continue in the benchmarking channel.
